title: Which sources to prefer, best first
note: Read by the scout and the planner. A higher rank is a better place to look first and a stronger kind of evidence; a lower rank is still shown, labelled, and never hidden. Ranking is advice for the plan: every claim still needs a word-for-word quote from a page that was read.

ranks.kind: the subject's own site, filings and press releases (the company's own words)
ranks.examples: investor-relations pages, newsroom, EDGAR filings (10-K, 10-Q, 8-K), releases on PR Newswire, Business Wire or GlobeNewswire
ranks.why: primary: the subject speaking for itself, wherever it is hosted; a filing or release is primary only if the company is its author

ranks.examples: sec.gov filings by others about the company, patent offices, court and government registers

ranks.kind: a major publication reporting on the company
ranks.examples: WSJ, Bloomberg, Reuters, AP, FT, NYT, CNBC
ranks.why: secondary: independent but second-hand, because it cites the filings and releases above; name it, and prefer the primary document it cites

ranks.examples: OpenAlex, arXiv, publisher pages, standards bodies
ranks.why: stable records with exact dates and authors

ranks.examples: aggregators, blogs, forums, analyst sites, social media
ranks.why: weakest; use only to find a better source
general-purpose knowledge only (a founding year, a definition). Never a source for a key development or news about a company.

suggest_correction_when: the scout finds nothing for something the question names (a year, a document, an event) but finds a close match nearby (the same document for another year, the same event under another name)
never: copy a value, date or quote from a search result into the plan: results only show what exists and where
